author: AfricanFeminism
title: Eight Years in Prison for Fighting Anti-Black Racism in Tunisia: Free Saadia Mosbah!
content:
For years, Saadia Mosbah has been one of the leading voices against anti-Black racism in Tunisia. As president of the anti-racism organisation Mnemty, she has stood up for Black Tunisians and Black migrants alike. When

 

violence against Black migrants escalated

 after President Kais Saied’s February 2023 statement against African migrants, she became a target of online hate campaigns.




On May 6, 2024, she was arrested. On March 19, 2026, she was sentenced to eight years in prison and a heavy fine on charges of money laundering and illicit enrichment. On June 23, the Tunis Court of Appeals upheld her conviction, along with those of five Mnemty colleagues and associates. A final appeal, filed on June 29, is now before the Court of Cassation.




Human rights movements and organisations,

 

including Amnesty International

, have denounced the irregularities in the proceedings and the lack of evidence for the alleged offences. They have also raised the alarm over the racist treatment and violence Saadia has reportedly suffered in detention.




Saadia’s case sits within a wider pattern of repression. Since President Kais Saied seized sweeping powers in July 2021, Tunisia has slid back into authoritarian rule. Since May 2024, the month of Saadia’s arrest, the authorities have waged

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Morocco’s First Woman Prime Minister and the Terms of Freedom
content:
Something changes when a woman occupies an office men have treated as their natural inheritance. Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri’s 

appointment

 on 29 September 2026 makes that change visible in Morocco. For women whose competence is routinely scrutinised, the pleasure is neither naïve nor trivial.




But the woman forming a government and the woman labouring in the fields, raising children without pay and denied an equal share of her inheritance encounter power differently. Representation changes who governs; emancipation changes what all women have the power to do. That distinction shifts our attention from PM Mansouri’s gender to the politics of the centre-right

 Party of Authenticity and Modernity (PAM

)

, which she leads. Will its programme redistribute the resources and rights on which women’s freedom depends?




The history beneath the headline




Calling women’s leadership foreign to Morocco requires forgetting its history. Historian Osire Glacier 

documents

 women’s authority long before the contemporary premiership. Kenza al Awrabiya, the Amazigh mother of Idris II, helped secure the Idrisid dynasty, founded in the late eighth century in what is now Morocco. Zaynab al Nafzawiyya influenced eleventh-century Almoravid politics around Aghmat, near Marrakech. Sayyida al Hurra governed Tétouan, a city in northern Morocco, during the sixteenth century. author: AfricanFeminism
title: Feminist Spaces: Abusive Power and the Accountability We Owe
content:
Feminist spaces are not toxic. Feminism is not toxic. Accountability is not toxic.




So, what is?




This began as my rage, but now it is my love letter to the movement.




A call to do better. To be better. To build spaces worthy of the feminism we claim.




This piece is born from my rage. From the nights I spent questioning whether I was too sensitive, too difficult, too much. From the moments I swallowed my truth because speaking it would cost me opportunities, contracts, references, relationships, or my place in the movement. From the realization that I was being asked to trade my voice for access, my dignity for opportunity, my growth for loyalty and the truth is… I am done trading.




I know I am not alone. This is not just my story. It is the story of countless women, feminists, workers, and young people who have been asked to choose between their voice and their livelihood, between their dignity and their place in the room.




Maybe you know this feeling. The tightness in your chest before a meeting. The way you edit yourself mid-sentence. The calculations you make: 

If I say this, will I lose that contract? That reference? That place at the table?
